research.job_description_summary: TCS hires fresh graduates (B.E./B.Tech., M.E./M.Tech., MCA, M.Sc./M.S.) through one integrated National Qualifier Test (NQT) held on TCS iON. Part A (Foundation, 75 min) covers numerical, verbal and reasoning ability; Part B (Advanced, 115 min) covers advanced quantitative and reasoning ability and 90 minutes of advanced coding. Performance in the test routes candidates to the Prime, Digital or Ninja track (listed fresher CTC: Prime 9.0 LPA, Digital 7.0 LPA, Ninja 3.36 LPA for UG), followed by interviews.
required_skills: Advanced coding in C, C++, Java, Python or C#
limitations: The official TCS NQT page lists the test structure and CTC but names no job roles, no interview rounds and no 2026 dates; interview-round details come from secondary sources and candidate reports.
Sources disagree on whether Ninja candidates face a coding section and on whether the coding section has 2 or 3 problems; coding rounds are therefore labeled REPORTED, not DOCUMENTED.

Candidate reports are anonymous public summaries (careerforfreshers.com, prepinsta.com) and cannot be independently verified; they are marked UNVERIFIED. Report months (April to August 2026) come from the source text, but the article publication dates are not shown.
The 'real questions' lists on jobrise.io and hirist.tech cite no candidate reports, so they were used only as topic context, not as evidence that TCS asked a question.
Several items come from a 2023 GeeksforGeeks Digital-track report and are labeled low confidence.
Ninja, Digital and Prime are hiring tracks, not official job titles; the title Assistant System Engineer comes from a candidate report.
Aptitude MCQs and the two Prime coding problems marked D are original practice items, not reported questions.
Cutoff percentiles and track-wise round counts quoted by secondary guides are unofficial and were not used as facts.
Evidence from other tracks: a few questions rest on reports from a different TCS track or on a 2023 report; they are marked NEEDS_REVIEW or low confidence and noted in each question.

Coverage gaps: aptitude has only a handful of practice items against a much larger real test; graphs, trees, dynamic programming and system design are not covered because no 2026 report in the sources mentions them for freshers.

questions.prompt: A retailer marks a product 25% above its cost price and then gives a 10% discount on the marked price. What is the retailer's profit percentage?
questions.relevance_to_role: The official TCS NQT page lists Numerical, Verbal and Reasoning ability as the Foundation section taken by every fresher.

rubric.criterion: Shows the working or reasoning method

follow_ups: What discount would make the profit exactly 10%?
common_mistakes: Applying the discount to the cost price
questions.notes: Section names and durations come from the official TCS NQT page; the item itself is an original practice question.

mcq.explanation: Take cost = 100. Marked price = 125. Selling price = 125 x 0.90 = 112.5. Profit = 12.5%.
mcq.distractor_notes: Adding +25% and -10% gives 15%, the most common trap. 10% ignores the markup. 17.5% is a plausible-looking miscalculation.

questions.prompt: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence: 'The team of engineers ___ presenting its design to the client tomorrow.'
questions.relevance_to_role: The official TCS NQT page lists Numerical, Verbal and Reasoning ability as the Foundation section taken by every fresher.

rubric.criterion: Shows the working or reasoning method

follow_ups: How would the verb change in 'The engineers on the team ___ presenting'?
common_mistakes: Matching the verb to 'engineers' instead of 'team'
questions.notes: Section names and durations come from the official TCS NQT page; the item itself is an original practice question.

mcq.explanation: 'Team' is a collective noun treated as a single unit here, and the pronoun 'its' confirms a singular subject, so 'is' fits.
mcq.distractor_notes: "are" agrees with "engineers" instead of the singular subject "team". "were" is the wrong tense for "tomorrow". "have" does not fit with "presenting".

questions.prompt: Find the next number in the series: 3, 6, 11, 18, 27, ?
questions.relevance_to_role: The official TCS NQT page lists Numerical, Verbal and Reasoning ability as the Foundation section taken by every fresher.

rubric.criterion: Shows the working or reasoning method

follow_ups: What is the 10th term of this series?
questions.notes: Section names and durations come from the official TCS NQT page; the item itself is an original practice question.

mcq.explanation: Differences are 3, 5, 7, 9, so the next difference is 11 and 27 + 11 = 38.
mcq.distractor_notes: 36 repeats the last difference of 9 instead of continuing the pattern 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. 39 and 40 are arithmetic slips.

questions.prompt: Worker A can finish a job in 12 days and worker B can finish the same job in 18 days. Working together, how many days do they need?
questions.relevance_to_role: The official TCS NQT page lists Numerical, Verbal and Reasoning ability as the Foundation section taken by every fresher.

rubric.criterion: Shows the working or reasoning method

follow_ups: If B leaves after 4 days of joint work, how long does A need to finish alone?
common_mistakes: Adding the days instead of the rates
questions.notes: Section names and durations come from the official TCS NQT page; the item itself is an original practice question.

mcq.explanation: Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 of the job per day, so the time is 36/5 = 7.2 days.
mcq.distractor_notes: Averaging 12 and 18 gives 15, which is not offered; 6, 7.5 and 8 are estimates that ignore adding the work rates.

questions.prompt: Riya walks 5 km north, turns right and walks 3 km, then turns right again and walks 5 km. How far, and in which direction, is she from her starting point?
questions.relevance_to_role: The official TCS NQT page lists Numerical, Verbal and Reasoning ability as the Foundation section taken by every fresher.

rubric.criterion: Shows the working or reasoning method

follow_ups: What if the last turn had been to the left?
common_mistakes: Confusing which way a right turn points
questions.notes: Section names and durations come from the official TCS NQT page; the item itself is an original practice question.

mcq.explanation: North 5, then east 3, then south 5 brings her back to the starting latitude, 3 km east of the start.
mcq.distractor_notes: 3 km west reverses east and west. 5 km north ignores the last leg. 8 km east adds the distances instead of tracking position.

questions.prompt: A number is given as a string of up to 100 digits. Number its positions from the left starting at 1. Return the sum of digits at odd positions minus the sum of digits at even positions.
questions.relevance_to_role: A candidate-reported NQT coding problem; checks careful string handling when the number does not fit in a normal integer type.
questions.expected_answer: Iterate over characters, add digits at even 0-based indexes and subtract digits at odd 0-based indexes.

rubric.criterion: Reads input as string, not integer

follow_ups: How would you solve it if the number was a stream of unknown length?
questions.notes: Reported by one candidate on the Prepinsta page (page dated 2026-02-25, candidate report undated). Wording, limits and samples are original.

coding.problem_statement: Given a non-negative number as a string of at most 100 digits, return (sum of digits at odd positions) - (sum of digits at even positions), counting positions from the left starting at 1.
coding.expected_algorithm: Read as a string and add or subtract each digit by index parity.

questions.prompt: Given an integer n, decide whether it is prime. Your solution must run fast for n up to one billion.
questions.relevance_to_role: Prime-number programs are a frequent fresher coding and interview request in 2026 candidate reports.
questions.expected_answer: Handle n < 2, then test divisors from 2 while i*i <= n.
follow_ups: How would you list all primes below 10^7?
questions.notes: Reported in at least two 2026 candidate reports summarized by the source; exact limits are original.

coding.problem_statement: Given an integer n, print Yes if n is prime, otherwise print No.
coding.expected_algorithm: Trial division up to sqrt(n), skipping even numbers after 2.

questions.prompt: Given an array of integers, find its second largest distinct value, or report that none exists.
questions.relevance_to_role: Reported in a 2026 candidate account; tests single-pass reasoning and duplicate handling.
questions.expected_answer: Keep two variables; update the second only when a value is strictly between the two.
follow_ups: How would you find the k-th largest distinct value?
common_mistakes: Returning the maximum twice for duplicates
questions.notes: Reported by one candidate (April 2026) in a public report summarized by the source.

coding.problem_statement: Given an array of n integers, print the second largest distinct value. Print -1 if there is no such value.
coding.input_format: Line 1: n. Line 2: n space-separated integers.
coding.expected_algorithm: Single pass tracking the largest and second largest distinct values.

questions.prompt: Reverse a given line of text without relying on a built-in reverse helper.
questions.relevance_to_role: String reversal appears in several 2026 candidate reports for both the test and the interview.
questions.expected_answer: Swap characters from both ends moving inward until the pointers cross.
follow_ups: Reverse the order of words instead of characters.
common_mistakes: Using slicing when the interviewer asked for a manual approach
questions.notes: Reported in at least two 2026 candidate accounts summarized by the source.

coding.problem_statement: Given a line of printable ASCII text (spaces allowed), print it reversed character by character.
coding.expected_algorithm: Two-pointer swap on a character array.

questions.prompt: Compare a list and a tuple in Python. When would you pick each?
questions.relevance_to_role: Reported in a candidate account where Python was the preferred language; checks language fundamentals.
questions.expected_answer: Lists are mutable and tuples are immutable. Tuples whose elements are hashable can be dictionary keys or set members, and they signal fixed data. Lists suit collections that change; tuples suit records and return values.
follow_ups: Can a tuple contain a list? What happens if you modify that list?
common_mistakes: Saying tuples are always faster without caveats
Forgetting a tuple can hold mutable items
questions.notes: Reported by two sources; the exact interview year of one report is not given.

questions.subtopic: Call by value and call by reference
questions.prompt: Explain call by value and call by reference. How does your preferred language handle argument passing?
questions.relevance_to_role: Reported in a technical-interview account; tests how the candidate reasons about function arguments.
questions.expected_answer: Call by value copies the argument, so changes inside the function do not affect the caller. Call by reference passes an alias, so changes are visible to the caller. C++ supports both through references and pointers; Java always passes values, and for objects the value is a copy of the reference; Python passes object references.
follow_ups: Does swapping two ints inside a function change them in the caller? In C, C++ and Java?
common_mistakes: Saying Java passes objects by reference

questions.prompt: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
questions.relevance_to_role: Reported in a technical-interview account; polymorphism is a core entry-level topic.
questions.expected_answer: Overloading is multiple methods with the same name and different parameter lists in the same scope, resolved at compile time. Overriding redefines an inherited method with the same signature in a subclass, resolved at run time. Static, private and final methods cannot be overridden.
follow_ups: Can you overload by return type alone?
common_mistakes: Claiming return type alone distinguishes overloads

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a primary key and a unique key?
questions.relevance_to_role: Reported in two candidate accounts; key constraints are a standard DBMS screening question.
questions.expected_answer: A table has one primary key and it cannot be NULL; it uniquely identifies each row. A table can have several unique keys, and most databases allow NULLs in them (how many NULLs differs by vendor). Both enforce uniqueness and are backed by an index.
follow_ups: Can a foreign key reference a unique key?
common_mistakes: Saying a unique key can never hold NULL
Saying a table can have many primary keys

questions.prompt: What are the necessary conditions for a deadlock, and how can a system prevent one?
questions.relevance_to_role: Reported in a Ninja-track candidate account; OS concepts are tested at fresher level.
questions.expected_answer: Four conditions must hold together: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Prevention breaks one of them, for example by acquiring all resources at once or imposing a global resource ordering. Avoidance (banker's algorithm) and detection plus recovery are alternatives.
follow_ups: Give a small two-thread example of a deadlock.

questions.prompt: Walk me through your final-year or best project: the problem, your role, the technologies you chose and why, and one challenge you solved.
questions.relevance_to_role: Candidates across several 2026 accounts were asked to explain a project and its technologies.
questions.expected_answer: A clear problem statement, the candidate's own contribution, justified technology choices, the output or result, and one concrete technical challenge with how it was solved. The interviewer will probe any detail on the resume.
follow_ups: What would you redesign if you rebuilt it today?
common_mistakes: Unable to explain the code they list
questions.notes: Reported repeatedly across the sources; counted as five report mentions.

questions.prompt: Are you willing to relocate to any TCS location in India? If you have constraints, how would you explain them?
questions.relevance_to_role: Relocation came up in several candidate-reported HR rounds.
questions.expected_answer: A direct, honest answer. If willing, say so and briefly explain why; if there are constraints, state them calmly rather than hiding them, and ask clarifying questions about the terms.
follow_ups: What would make you hesitate about relocating?
common_mistakes: Giving a yes you do not mean
questions.notes: Relocation confirmed in three accounts on careerforfreshers.com. The service-agreement part was removed because it was not found in that source.

questions.prompt: How is working at a service-based company different from a product-based company, and why does a service company appeal to you?
questions.relevance_to_role: Reported in an HR-round account; tests career awareness and motivation.
questions.expected_answer: Service companies build and run solutions for client businesses across many domains and technologies; product companies build and own a single product line. A good answer is balanced, names real benefits such as domain variety and structured training, and avoids disparaging either.
follow_ups: Where do you see yourself in five years?

questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you failed at something. What did you learn?
questions.relevance_to_role: Reported in two candidate accounts; entry-level interviews check maturity and learning attitude.
questions.expected_answer: A real, specific failure, owned honestly, followed by the behavior change it caused.

rubric.criterion: Own actions and reasoning are clear

follow_ups: How did you apply that lesson later?
common_mistakes: Choosing a failure with no learning

behavioral.star_guidance: Situation: what you attempted. Task: your goal. Action: what you did and how you responded to the setback. Result: what changed and what you do differently now.
negative_signals: Picks a trivial or fake failure
